name: Tailwind CSS
one_liner: Utility-class CSS framework that moves styling decisions into markup.
what_it_is: A CSS framework that ships a large set of single-purpose utility classes — padding, colour, flex, typography — which you compose directly in markup, plus a build step that strips every class you did not use. It deliberately does not ship pre-built components like a button or a card; it gives you the scale, not the parts.
why_it_matters: Tailwind is the clearest example of a shift many experienced CSS developers sat out. The standard objection — that utility classes in markup are inline styles with extra steps — is reasonable, and it lost on practical grounds rather than aesthetic ones. Constraining developers to a fixed token scale prevents the slow entropy that afflicts hand-written stylesheets, and colocating style with markup dissolves the naming problem that consumed a decade of CSS architecture argument (BEM, OOCSS, SMACSS). If your view of styling settled around Sass and BEM, this is the specific thing worth re-examining — not because it is popular, but because the problem it solves is one you probably still have.
suitable_for: Teams that want a shared design-token scale without having to author one
Component-based codebases where markup and style are edited together
Developers for whom naming CSS classes is the slow part of styling
not_suitable_for: Codebases that must emit semantic, framework-neutral HTML for third parties to consume or restyle
Teams with a mature existing design system in plain CSS, where migration cost usually exceeds the benefit
Projects where markup is authored by people who do not run the build — CMS templates edited by non-developers
HTML email, which cannot rely on the build step
